case_info.scenario: An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

dialogue_history.text: I disagree with initiating ambrisentan and tadalafil as the next step. In hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), pulmonary hypertension is often due to high-output heart failure from hepatic arteriovenous malformations or pulmonary arterial hypertension from pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs), and specific vasodilator therapy can be dangerous without confirming the exact mechanism. The immediate priority should be a CT angiogram to evaluate for treatable PAVMs, as embolization is the definitive therapy.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

[Case]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.
